TODDLER 6 · LESSON 12

Vehicles and Sounds for 2-Year-Olds

Age 2 YearsSubject Talk & ExploreClass Toddler 6Duration 3–5 minutes

Beep beep! Vroom! Choo choo! At two, vehicles are sound machines on wheels, wings and water — and this class meets twenty of them, with big cards and three quick games.

Nothing to read and nothing to test. A sound in, a sound back — a tap, a point or a giggle all count. A few playful minutes is plenty.

Start Class ↓Beep beep first. Works every time.

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the vehicle cards together.

The vehicle cards print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed and cut, they become a week of sorting, naming and sound-making at the kitchen table.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twenty, two to a page. Cut them out together, naming each vehicle as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Make the sounds

    Hold up a card and make its sound — beep, vroom, choo choo, nee-naw — then let your toddler conduct: card up, sound on.

  3. 03

    Sort by where they go

    Sort the cards into little fleets: things on the road, things in the sky, things on the water. Where-it-goes is real sorting work.

  4. 04

    Count the wheels

    Pick three cards and count the wheels on each — one, two, lots. Counting inside a favourite topic is the friendliest maths there is.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Vehicle hunt.

Look out the window or take a walk. Spot a car, bus or truck and name it together.

Try one today

  • Count the buses you see.
  • Listen for a beep.
  • Pretend to drive a car.
  • Make a train go choo choo.
  • Spot something that flies.

Keep it playful and stay close by. One spotted bus is a complete class.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

Tips for Parents

A toddler who answers every vehicle with vroom is doing the class exactly right. Any sound back is them talking.

Bring sounds into the body — steer a car, chug your arms like a train, rock like a boat. Movement helps words stick.

Repeats are the point. The tenth choo choo is still funny — and still teaching.

Age ranges are a guide. Go at your child’s pace.

    Car — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the vehicle your toddler already announces daily and builds it out: the vroom, the wheels, the window-counting game, with the driveway rule taught early and calmly.

    What is this?

    A car is a four-wheeled machine that carries people and goes vroom — the word most two-year-olds own before any other vehicle name.

    What does it mean?

    Car is often a first two-consonant word, said at full volume from a strapped-in seat. Naming what passes by is your toddler’s first independent labelling of the moving world.

    What does the child need to know?

    Wheels are the detail that hooks toddlers: round, turning, endlessly fascinating. Say "wheels go round" as you point and a describing word hops aboard for free.

    Why this matters

    Cars pass constantly, so this word gets rehearsed dozens of times a day without a single minute of table time. High-frequency words are the fastest words a toddler banks.

    What it teaches

    Vocabulary growth through daily labelling, counting chances with every passing car, and the first road-awareness words — car, stop, hold hands.

    Words to learn

    carvroomwheelsroadfastbeep

    Say this to your child

    “"A car! Vroom, vroom. Can you say car? Where are its wheels — can you point? Wheels go round and round. Beep beep! Here comes another one."”

    Step by step

    1. Hold up the card and say car, then vroom — with a forward roll of your hands like turning wheels.
    2. Add the sound effects: vroom for driving, beep beep for saying hello. Let your toddler choose which the car is doing.
    3. Hunt cars in books and toy boxes first, then take the game to the front window and count the cars that pass — one car, two cars.
    4. When your toddler shouts car! for every single vehicle including lorries, take the shout — accuracy arrives later, enthusiasm is the engine.
    5. Park the game at the day’s real edges: vroom into the car seat, beep beep at the car park, one window count before dinner.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card is labelled Car with the words Beep beep beneath — find the label together, then find the beep-beep words and make the sound they promise.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the car?" "What does the car say?" "Can you find the wheels?" "How many cars can we count from the window?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Car!" shouted at volume from the window, plus a vroom with pushing hands. Some toddlers will beep at every doorway for a week — greetings are the game they took home.

    Out in the real world

    Real cars are the lesson’s forever stage: the drive to nursery, the walk to the shop, the parked cars on the street. Name them, count them, hold hands near them.

    Try it together

    Rug traffic: push toy cars along taped roads on the floor, vrooming at each junction and stopping at the cushion roundabout. Stop and go is the game — and the street rule in training wheels.

    Understanding check

    Ask what a car says and where its wheels are. A vroom plus a wheel-point passes. Then watch the window tomorrow — unprompted car-shouting means the word has gone permanent.

    Parent tips

    Count aloud even if counting means nothing yet — the rhythm of one, two lands long before the numbers do. Keep vroom for cars and give lorries their own lesson; sorting comes later, noise comes now.

    Staying safe

    Driveways are the most dangerous metres in a toddler’s day: hold hands in every car park, and teach early that parked cars can wake up and move with no warning at all.

    This lesson pairs with the Car flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Bus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson rides the toddler’s own experience: the bus they have sat on, the song they half-know, and the doors that open and shut — naming each part as it happens.

    What is this?

    A bus is a big long vehicle that carries lots of people and goes beep beep — usually the machine a two-year-old has physically ridden.

    What does it mean?

    The bus is vocabulary attached to memory: the bumpy seat, the tall windows, the beep of the doors. Experience-backed words stick faster than any picture alone.

    What does the child need to know?

    The bus song about the wheels going round is the teaching tool built into this card — every verse is a body part or a bus part, sung while pointing at both.

    Why this matters

    Buses run on schedules and streets, so sightings are daily and the song is everywhere. The word rehearses itself at every window.

    What it teaches

    Song-and-gesture pairing, part-naming (wheels, doors, windows), and the first feel of public transport as a normal, nameable part of life.

    Words to learn

    busbeepwheelsdoorsridepeople

    Say this to your child

    “"A bus! Beep beep! The bus is big and long. Can you roll your wheels — round and round? The bus carries lots of people, and the doors go open and shut."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say bus, then beep beep — two cheerful toots with your palm as the horn.
    2. Sing the bus’s own song while your finger taps the wheels on the card, then roll your hands round and round together.
    3. Hunt buses in books and toy baskets, then take up a window post and wait for a real one to rumble past.
    4. When your toddler answers with a beep, a wheel-roll or the first da of the song, join in exactly where they are and carry the verse.
    5. Give the bus its weekly job: if a real route runs nearby, stand at the stop once this week and watch the doors open and shut in person.

    Look closer at the picture

    Two words to find on this card: the label Bus and the sound words Beep beep. Point at each one, then ask where the wheels sit on the picture.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the bus?" "What does the bus say?" "Can you roll your hands like wheels?" "Who rides on the bus with us?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Bus!" with a palm-toot, or the round-and-round arm rolls started without any sound. Some toddlers will demand the song every bus sighting for months — let them; the verses are vocabulary.

    Out in the real world

    The real bus stop is this card’s graduation hall: watch a bus arrive, beep at it, name the wheels and the doors, then wave it off. If you ride one, the card comes too.

    Try it together

    Chair bus: line up kitchen chairs, take the driver’s seat, and sing the whole song with gestures — wheels, doors, mummies, daddies. Ticket-clipping with a pretend punch adds a job for small hands.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the bus says and what the wheels do. A beep plus round-and-round hands passes. At the next real sighting, a pointed finger and a toot means the card rode all the way home.

    Parent tips

    The song does the heavy lifting, so learn two verses well rather than five badly. Bus routes beat zoo trips for value: the same teaching opportunity drives past every day of the week.

    Staying safe

    At the stop, stand back from the kerb with a firm hand on your toddler — buses swing in close and their wheels hide small feet. On board, everyone sits or holds on from the first bump.

    This lesson pairs with the Bus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Truck — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gives the road’s biggest regular visitor its due: the rumble, the trailer, the guessing game about what it carries — all from the safety of the window.

    What is this?

    A truck is a big vehicle with a trailer that goes rumble — a low rolling noise toddlers can feel in their chests when one passes close.

    What does it mean?

    Inside this card waits a toddler’s first two-word phrase: big truck. Point, pause, and say it slowly once — the pause is where the phrase assembles itself.

    What does the child need to know?

    Trucks carry things — bricks, sand, food, mysterious crates. The guessing game has no wrong answers at two, and every guess is a chance to talk.

    Why this matters

    Trucks pass less often than cars but hit harder when they do: the rarity and the rumble make each sighting an event worth naming out loud.

    What it teaches

    Size vocabulary (big, biggest), imitation of a low sustained sound, and early guessing-and-telling — prediction talk in its first clothes.

    Words to learn

    truckrumblebigtrailercarryload

    Say this to your child

    “"A truck! Rumble, rumble — so big. Can you make the rumble? Down deep, like this. What is the truck carrying today? Bricks? Sand? Let us watch and guess."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say truck, then rumble — a low chesty noise, slower and deeper than the car’s vroom.
    2. Rumble together while pushing a toy truck slowly across the rug: big trucks take up space and take their time.
    3. Hunt trucks in books and on the road from the window; when a real one passes, guess together what the trailer might be carrying.
    4. When your toddler delivers a brrr or a deep mmm, accept it as the rumble and model the full version once, unhurried.
    5. Name every real truck this week — big truck, slow rumble — and let the phrase grow one word at a time.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the label Truck first, then the word Rumble underneath. Ask which part rolls along at the back — the trailer hitched behind is the detail to spot.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the truck?" "What does the truck say?" "Can you rumble like a big truck?" "What do you think is riding in the trailer?"

    What your child can say or do

    A chest-deep "rrrumble" or a pushed-out mmm — both are the truck voice arriving. Expect big truck to be applied to every large vehicle this week; the sorting refines itself later.

    Out in the real world

    Building sites, delivery mornings and motorway bridges are truck country. The pavements outside a building site are the premium seats — watch from behind the barriers, rumble on cue.

    Try it together

    Loading bay: fill a laundry basket with soft toys, let your toddler be the loader, then push the load across the room and tip it at the delivery point. Rumble mandatory, tipping ecstatic.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the truck says and whether it is big or little. A rumble plus big passes. Watch for the two-word phrase — big truck — arriving in real traffic this week.

    Parent tips

    Say the phrase slowly with a beat between the words: big… truck. Two-word phrases are built in pauses. The guessing game needs zero props and fills a supermarket queue.

    Staying safe

    Trucks have huge blind spots and long stopping distances — hold hands tight at any roadside, and watch them only from behind a fence, barrier or window, never from the kerb’s edge.

    This lesson pairs with the Truck flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Fire Truck — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns the loudest hero on the road into a rescue game: nee-naw around the rug, put the fire out, park the truck — with real sirens made familiar instead of scary.

    What is this?

    A fire truck is a big red rescue vehicle with a ladder and a siren that goes nee-naw — the sound toddlers master fastest of all the emergency noises.

    What does it mean?

    Nee-naw is a sliding two-note sound: pitch going up and down in one word. Sliding pitch is ear-training for the melody of speech, smuggled inside a siren.

    What does the child need to know?

    Fire trucks go out when there is a fire and help people — say that plainly. If real sirens worry your toddler, playing the sound on purpose shrinks it back down to size.

    Why this matters

    This is the deck’s drama card. The rescue game gives big feelings a storyline with an ending — fire out, everybody safe, truck parked — which is exactly how toddlers like their stories.

    What it teaches

    Pitch sliding and imitation, pretend play with a clear beginning and end, and the first idea of helpers — people whose job is to come when things go wrong.

    Words to learn

    fire trucknee-nawladderredrescuehero

    Say this to your child

    “"Fire truck! Nee-naw, nee-naw! Make the siren sound with me — up and down, nee-naw. The fire truck is red with a big ladder, and it drives fast to help. Rescue done — park the truck!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say fire truck, then nee-naw — let the sound slide up and down like the real siren.
    2. Push a cushion-fire-truck around the room together, nee-nawing at full volume until the pretend fire is out.
    3. Hunt fire trucks in books and toy boxes; find the ladder on each one and name it every time.
    4. When the siren comes out as a shriek or a whisper, take either — the slide matters more than the volume, and both are practice.
    5. Give rescues their slot this week: one fire, one rescue, one proud parking at the end, and the game closes itself neatly.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card says Fire Truck at the top with Nee-naw written beneath. Hunt for the siren words, then hunt for the ladder riding on top.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the fire truck?" "What does the fire truck say?" "Can you slide your nee-naw?" "What does the fire truck do after the fire is out?"

    What your child can say or do

    "NEE-NAW!" at whatever volume the day allows, or a sliding siren with no words at all. Some toddlers park their cushion trucks and announce done! — the ending is part of the story they learned.

    Out in the real world

    Real sirens pass on real streets. Name them calmly — "fire truck, nee-naw, going to help" — and the sound becomes information instead of alarm. Fire stations sometimes let small visitors sit in the truck; worth a call.

    Try it together

    Rescue the teddy: a bear is stuck on the sofa mountain, the fire truck rushes over, the ladder (your arm) extends, the bear is saved, the truck parks. A story with an ending, every single time.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the fire truck says and what colour it is. A nee-naw plus red passes. The deeper pass is the calm one — a real siren outside that gets a nod instead of a wobble.

    Parent tips

    Always finish the rescue and park the truck; the ending is what makes the game repeatable without escalation. When a real siren startles, narrate first and reassure second — information calms better than shushing.

    Staying safe

    Real fire trucks mean move aside and let them pass — teach that with a step to the side and a hand held. At home, cushion rescues stay on the floor; no climbing the actual furniture for the sake of a teddy.

    This lesson pairs with the Fire Truck flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Ambulance — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson pairs the siren with the care: the ambulance rushes, the paramedic checks, the teddy gets an examination and a cuddle — empathy practice wearing a siren.

    What is this?

    An ambulance is a white van with flashing lights that carries helpers to people who need a doctor — and it goes nee-naw, same notes as the fire truck.

    What does it mean?

    Same siren, different job: the ambulance and fire truck make one matching game and one first sorting lesson — two vehicles, one sound, two kinds of helping.

    What does the child need to know?

    Ambulances carry paramedics, whose whole job is helping people feel better. If your toddler ever rides one, the familiar sound and story make a hard day easier.

    Why this matters

    The caring play is the payload here: checking a teddy’s heartbeat, wrapping a blanket, delivering a cuddle. Naming the feeling of being helped is the beginning of empathy.

    What it teaches

    Pretend care routines, helping-vocabulary, sound matching between vehicles, and the reassurance that loud scary moments have calm, kind people inside them.

    Words to learn

    ambulancenee-nawhelpparamediccuddlebetter

    Say this to your child

    “"Ambulance! Nee-naw, nee-naw — the same song as the fire truck. The ambulance carries helpers. Teddy feels unwell — quick, drive over! Tap, tap… all better. What a kind paramedic."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say ambulance, then nee-naw — and note out loud that the fire truck makes the same sound.
    2. Run a teddy rescue: one bear feels poorly, the ambulance speeds over, and your toddler gives the check-up with a gentle tap-tap on the chest.
    3. Hunt ambulances in books and from the window; every real sighting gets its calm sentence — "ambulance, going to help someone."
    4. When the siren arrives but the caring does not, add the care yourself: wrap the teddy, ask your toddler to pat it better, and hand the role over next round.
    5. End every rescue with better now! and a cuddle — the happy ending is the lesson’s whole shape.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card is labelled Ambulance with Nee-naw underneath. Ask what colour the van is painted, then find the siren words and sing them once.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the ambulance?" "What does the ambulance say?" "Who rides inside the ambulance?" "Can you make teddy all better?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Nee-naw!" plus a teddy carried gently to the rug-clinic. Some toddlers will pat every family member better for a week — the caring half of the lesson is the one worth encouraging.

    Out in the real world

    Ambulances pass with their lights on; say the calm sentence each time. A first-aid open day or a ambulance visit at a toddler group is the big-field-trip version of this card.

    Try it together

    Teddy clinic: line up three unwell toys, drive the ambulance between them, and let your toddler diagnose each one — "pat, pat… better!" — before the last cuddle closes the clinic.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the ambulance says and who rides inside. A nee-naw plus helpers passes. The real test is a sibling or teddy taking a tumble — if the ambulance game appears to comfort them, the lesson bloomed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the helping bigger than the siren: the sound grabs attention, the caring holds it. If sirens in real life cause worry, act the sound out at home on your own terms until it shrinks.

    Staying safe

    Real ambulances mean step aside and let them through — hold hands and move to the wall together. If your own family ever needs one, name it plainly: loud noise, kind people, help coming.

    This lesson pairs with the Ambulance flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Police Car — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson lets your toddler run the roads for once: the woo-woo siren, the stop hand, the go wave — control games are the fastest way to a two-year-old’s heart.

    What is this?

    A police car is a marked car with lights on top that goes woo-woo — the third siren in the set, and the one with the bossy job.

    What does it mean?

    Three sirens, three vehicles: nee-naw twice and woo-woo once. Telling them apart is sound sorting, and the stop-and-go game adds the first traffic rules to the vocabulary.

    What does the child need to know?

    Police cars have bold stripes and bright lights so everyone can see them coming. The stripes are this card’s find-it detail once the siren has had its fun.

    Why this matters

    Being the traffic controller is power a toddler rarely gets, and the stop-and-go game teaches listening and impulse control while feeling like pure command.

    What it teaches

    Sound sorting across three sirens, stop-and-go impulse practice, and hand-signal play — following and giving simple instructions in the same round.

    Words to learn

    police carwoo-woostopgostripeslights

    Say this to your child

    “"Police car! Woo-woo, woo-woo. Can you make the siren? Look at its stripes — bold as anything. Now you are the police: hold up your hand — STOP! Wave — GO!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say police car, then woo-woo — and line it up beside the other two sirens for the family siren concert.
    2. Play traffic: you march, your toddler holds up a hand and calls stop!, then waves and calls go!. Swap roles after two rounds.
    3. Hunt police cars in books and from the window; find the stripes on each one — stripes are the uniform.
    4. When the siren comes out as woo or a long oooo, take it and slide it toward woo-woo once, then let their version stand.
    5. Keep the stop-go game alive all week at real transitions — stop at the door, go at the gate — and the card teaches at every doorway.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look for the label Police Car and the Woo-woo words below it. Then hunt the stripes that run along the side — the uniform is the detail.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the police car?" "What does the police car say?" "Can you show me stop with your hand?" "Can you find the stripes?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Woo-woo!" plus a stern little hand held flat — the stop gesture lands early and gets used on everyone, including the cat. Accept your arrests gracefully.

    Out in the real world

    Police cars pass with lights flashing; name them calmly like the other sirens. Community events sometimes park one for climbing-in — the closest a toddler gets to the driver’s seat.

    Try it together

    Siren concert: fire truck, ambulance and police car each get their sound, and your toddler points to the right card as you sing each siren. Three sounds, three cards, one proud conductor.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the police car says and what the hand says. A woo-woo plus a flat-palm stop passes fully. Watch for the stop hand used at a real kerb this week — that is the lesson working for you.

    Parent tips

    Swap director roles often: being stopped is as educational as stopping. Keep the tone playful — the game teaches listening, and no game survives becoming a lecture.

    Staying safe

    Police cars are helpers to know, but the deeper rule rides along: your toddler goes only with people you choose, and any grown-up who says keep it secret gets told to you straight away.

    This lesson pairs with the Police Car flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    Motorcycle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson leans into the corners: the vroom, the tilt, the two wheels — with the helmet sentence welded to the fun from the very first ride.

    What is this?

    A motorcycle is a fast two-wheeled machine with an engine that goes vroom — the loudest vroom in the set, often heard before it is seen.

    What does it mean?

    Same sound as the car, different body: the motorcycle comparison game (two wheels each, one has an engine) is your toddler’s first gentle vehicle sorting.

    What does the child need to know?

    The rider wears a helmet — say it in the same breath as the vroom, every time. Rules that arrive riding on excitement stick far better than rules delivered afterwards.

    Why this matters

    The lean is the hook: tilting your whole body into a corner is a big, satisfying movement that makes the sound impossible to say politely.

    What it teaches

    Sound imitation with body lean, two-versus-four comparison talk, and rule attachment — pairing one clear safety sentence to one exciting object.

    Words to learn

    motorcyclevroomfasthelmetleanengine

    Say this to your child

    “"Motorcycle! Vrooooom! Can you vroom? Lean into the corner — whoooa — and straighten up. Two wheels, fast as anything. And what does the rider wear? A helmet, every ride."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say motorcycle, then vroom — longer and louder than the car’s, with a lean of your whole body into an imaginary corner.
    2. Ride the rug: vroom down the straight, tilt at the cushion corner, straighten up and vroom on. Hand over the ride.
    3. Hunt motorcycles in books and from the window — the sound usually arrives first, so ask "what was that?" and go find it.
    4. When the vroom comes out as a motorboat hum or a yell, accept it and add the lean; the body carries the sound until the mouth catches up.
    5. Pair the sentence all week: motorcycle — helmet. Card, book, toy or real, the pairing never breaks.

    Look closer at the picture

    The label reads Motorcycle and the sound word Vroom sits beneath. Count the wheels with one finger — how many does it stand on?

    Ask your child

    "Where is the motorcycle?" "What does the motorcycle say?" "How many wheels does it have?" "What does the rider wear on their head?"

    What your child can say or do

    A long "vrrrOOOM" with a body tilt, or pure leaning with arms out. Expect helmet talk to surface at odd moments — at the bike rack, on the trike — the pairing took.

    Out in the real world

    Motorcycles pass with that unmistakable growl; each one is a listen-and-find game. Parked ones at the shops show off the helmet on the mirror — point at it every time.

    Try it together

    Ride-and-lean circuit: cushions as corners, a scarf as the finish-line flag, and one vrooming lap after another. The flag-waver job rotates, and so does the exhaustion.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the motorcycle says and what the rider wears. A vroom plus helmet passes completely. On your toddler’s next trike ride, a requested helmet means the rule rode home.

    Parent tips

    Never drop the helmet line even when the game is loud — the whole design is that safety words ride on excitement. The comparison with the bicycle card is worth one session; keep it light.

    Staying safe

    Real motorcycles are fast and quiet-then-loud — hold hands when one approaches, and never let a toddler stand behind a parked one: engines and exhausts stay out of little hands.

    This lesson pairs with the Motorcycle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Bicycle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson matches the card to the machine in your own hallway: the bell, the pedals, the helmet — the bicycle is the vehicle toddlers can actually ride.

    What is this?

    A bicycle is a two-wheeled machine you pedal yourself, with a bell that goes ring ring — no engine, just legs.

    What does it mean?

    Bicycle is a long word and bike is the honest first version — both count fully. The hands-in-the-air pedalling turns the word into a whole-arm action.

    What does the child need to know?

    No engine makes the bicycle the quiet vehicle — legs and a bell. If there is a real bike or trike at home, this card is its instruction manual.

    Why this matters

    The bicycle is the set’s do-it-yourself vehicle: your toddler can ring a real bell and turn real pedals, which makes the learning physical instead of pictured.

    What it teaches

    Action-sound pairing (pedal and ring), ownership of a vehicle they can actually operate, and the helmet rule attached to their own real rides.

    Words to learn

    bicyclebikeringpedalsbellhelmet

    Say this to your child

    “"A bicycle! Ring ring! Can you ring the bell? Now pedal with your hands — round and round. Your bike has two wheels, just like this one. Helmet on — ready to ride!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say bicycle — then bike, and let both words live happily together.
    2. Pedal the air with your hands while going round and round, then ring ring with an invisible bell. Your toddler will take over the bell.
    3. Hunt bicycles in books, then bring the card to the real one in the hall and match card to machine, wheel to wheel.
    4. When bike arrives long before bicycle, celebrate bike — the short word is the door, the long one walks in later.
    5. Attach the card to real rides all week: helmet on, bell rung, card waved goodbye to at the gate.

    Look closer at the picture

    On this card the label is Bicycle and the bell words Ring ring sit under it. Find the pedals, find the bell, then count the wheels one more time.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the bicycle?" "What does the bell say?" "Can you pedal the air?" "What do we put on our head before we ride?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Ring ring!" with a thumb-flick bell, or bike! announced at the hall cupboard. Expect the bell sound on everything — spoons, doors, your nose. Bells are contagious.

    Out in the real world

    The park, the school run and the bike shed are bicycle country. Parked bikes show real pedals, real bells, real helmets — a three-point tour every visit.

    Try it together

    Bell-and-go circuit: your toddler rings, you push the trike or the ride-on one lap, ring again, another lap. The bell becomes the accelerator — and the giggle lever.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the bell says and what the rider wears. A ring ring plus helmet passes. The real pass: next ride-out, the bell gets rung before the wheels turn.

    Parent tips

    Say bike and bicycle both, warmly, whenever the machine appears — no correcting, just both versions on offer. Keep the card near the helmet; storage is curriculum.

    Staying safe

    Helmet on before wheels turn, every ride, no exceptions — and the rule starts with the grown-up’s bike too, because toddlers copy what they see, not what they hear.

    This lesson pairs with the Bicycle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Train — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson builds a train out of kitchen chairs: chugging, tickets, one engine and a station — with tracks-not-roads as the quiet fact riding along.

    What is this?

    A train is a long vehicle that runs on tracks and goes choo choo — a chain of carriages your toddler can count, hook and drive.

    What does it mean?

    One train, many carriages: the train is where part-and-whole shows up in a toddler’s favourite machine. Counting carriages is counting with a purpose.

    What does the child need to know?

    Trains go on tracks, cars go on roads — one sentence, said while pointing at wheels and rails, files itself away. Real platforms have the loud announcements and the gap.

    Why this matters

    No other card arrives with its own soundtrack quite like this one. Few games convert a rainy afternoon into forty minutes of organised noise as reliably as the chair-train.

    What it teaches

    Sequencing and pretend roles (driver, passengers, inspector), sound chains in rhythm, and the tracks-versus-roads distinction that organises the whole vehicle world.

    Words to learn

    trainchoo chootrackcarriagestationticket

    Say this to your child

    “"A train! Choo choo! Can you chug with me? Chugga-chugga-choo-choo! Here comes our train, running on tracks, not roads. All aboard! Tickets, please — next stop, the kitchen!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say train, then choo choo — with slow arm-wheels and a chuffing breath.
    2. Build the chair-train: kitchen chairs in a line, your toddler as the engine at the front, chugging around the room together.
    3. Hunt trains in books and toy boxes; count the carriages on each one — one, two, three.
    4. When the sound comes out as a chuff or a woo, take it and add one more choo; chains grow one link at a time.
    5. Ride the real thing this week if you can — the platform gap, the whoosh, the doors — or run the chair-train daily and sell tickets.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows the label Train with Choo choo written below. Ask how many carriages are hooked behind the engine, then count them together.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the train?" "What does the train say?" "Does the train go on tracks or on the road?" "Who is driving our train today?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Choo choo!" plus a chugging march, or a ticket held up high for clipping. Expect the chair-train to run daily for weeks — engines do not retire quickly.

    Out in the real world

    Station platforms are train heaven: the announcement, the whoosh, the gap between train and edge. Behind the yellow line, hand in hand, the real thing beats every card.

    Try it together

    Full service: driver, passenger and ticket inspector, with paper tickets punched by a grown-up. The station is the sofa; the destination rotates; the announcements are yours to invent.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the train says and where trains go — tracks or roads. A choo choo plus tracks passes. The chair-train appearing unprompted is the distinction between passed and owned.

    Parent tips

    Let your toddler be the engine first — leading the chug gives them the tempo, and tempo is what makes the sound chain survive. Keep tickets scrap-paper simple; the punching is the joy.

    Staying safe

    Real platforms are the danger zone: hand held, behind the line, before the train is even visible. At home, the chair-train needs its cushions checked for trip-hazards before departure.

    This lesson pairs with the Train flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Tractor — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the farm’s slowest machine at its own pace: the put-put, the giant back wheels, the mud — with a country walk as the field trip that needs no planning.

    What is this?

    A tractor is a slow farm machine with huge back wheels that goes put-put — built for pulling, ploughing and generally being enormous.

    What does it mean?

    Put-put is a repeated beat rather than a word: your toddler is keeping rhythm, which is a different sound skill from the sliding sirens and long vrooms.

    What does the child need to know?

    Tractors work in fields and pull heavy things. Out on a country lane, or spotted through the windscreen, a real one working a field is the sighting this card exists for.

    Why this matters

    Slow is the novelty here — every other vehicle in the set is fast. The tractor teaches that machines have paces, and slow is funny when you perform it.

    What it teaches

    Rhythm-making with a repeated sound, size contrast (giant wheels, little cab), and farm-machine vocabulary that pays out at every country mile.

    Words to learn

    tractorput-putslowwheelsfieldpull

    Say this to your child

    “"A tractor! Put-put, put-put. Can you keep the beat? Slow and bumpy. Look at those giant back wheels — bigger than you! The tractor pulls heavy things in the field, slow and strong."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say tractor, then put-put — slow, bumpy and content, like an engine idling.
    2. Drive the rug at tractor speed: hands on a toy tractor, put-putting, taking the longest possible route to the shortest possible distance.
    3. Hunt tractors in books and from windows; find the giant back wheels — bigger than the whole front of the machine.
    4. When the put-put arrives as a pop or a slow brmm, accept it and keep the beat going; rhythm is caught, not corrected.
    5. Keep the speed joke alive all week — tractor-slow tidying, tractor-slow stairs — and say the sound at any real sighting.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the word Tractor on the label and Rumble beneath it. The giant back wheels are the detail — ask which wheels are the biggest on the card.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the tractor?" "What does the tractor say?" "Which wheels are the biggest?" "Is the tractor fast or slow?"

    What your child can say or do

    A steady "put-put-put" or a slow-motion march with sound effects. Some toddlers will adopt tractor pace for the whole walk home — the joke is the pace, and the pace is the point.

    Out in the real world

    Country walks, farm shops and harvest time are tractor season. A real one crossing the road in front of the car is the parade this card promised — count the wheels from your seat.

    Try it together

    Hauling yard: your toddler is the tractor, a rope or scarf is the hitch, and the trailer is a basket of toys pulled slowly across the rug. Put-put per step, unload at the barn (the sofa).

    Understanding check

    Ask what the tractor says and whether it is fast or slow. A put-put plus slow passes. Real-field sighting test: a pointed finger and a slow brmm from the car seat is full marks.

    Parent tips

    Exaggerate the slowness until it becomes the joke — toddlers learn pace by contrast with your speed. A farm trip turns this card into a whole day, but a field behind a fence does the same job.

    Staying safe

    Real tractors are working machines with moving parts and blind spots — watch from the car, the gate or the footpath, and never climb on parked ones, however perfect the seat looks.

    This lesson pairs with the Tractor flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Excavator — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson surrenders to the inevitable: your toddler loves diggers. Scoop, swing, dump, repeat — with both words on offer, digger for now and excavator for delight.

    What is this?

    An excavator is a digging machine with a long arm and a bucket that goes dig dig — called a digger by everyone under four.

    What does it mean?

    Two names for one machine is a first synonym: digger and excavator. Say both without pressure — the long word is a treat, the short one is the working vocabulary.

    What does the child need to know?

    The arm scoops, swings and dumps — three verbs in one machine. Pair the card with any digging toy and the afternoon arranges itself; a bowl of dry cereal upgrades it further.

    Why this matters

    This is the card a two-year-old requests at breakfast, lunch and dinner. Favoured cards do the teaching on their own; your job is to keep the scoop moving.

    What it teaches

    Action verbs (dig, scoop, swing, dump), fine-motor scooping practice, and the pride of owning a long word most grown-ups fumble.

    Words to learn

    excavatordiggerdigscoopbucketdump

    Say this to your child

    “"Digger! Or — excavator, if you are feeling fancy. Dig dig dig! Can you scoop? Swing the arm… and DUMP! Look at those wheels and that long arm. Again!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say digger, then excavator slowly, like a treat — and dig dig with your arm as the bucket.
    2. Scoop together: spoon-digger into a bowl of dry rice or cereal — scoop, swing, dump — narrating each verb as it happens.
    3. Hunt diggers in books and from windows; real excavators on building sites are visible from a long way off, which helps.
    4. When your toddler says brrm or digs without the sound, supply the dig dig and cheer the digging — verbs land one at a time.
    5. Keep the bowl and spoon set up this week; a standing digging station means the card teaches itself between meals.

    Look closer at the picture

    The label says Excavator and the words Dig dig sit under it. Follow the long arm with one finger — where does it end? In the bucket.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the excavator?" "What does the arm do?" "Can you scoop and dump?" "Which word is longer — digger or excavator?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Dig dig!" with a spoon, or the full excavator attempt which lands as ek-ka-vator and is entirely wonderful. The dump is always louder than the dig.

    Out in the real world

    Building sites, roadworks and sandpits are excavator country. Behind the hoarding, watch a real arm work one full cycle — scoop, swing, dump — and the card comes home pre-taught.

    Try it together

    Sandpit site: bucket as the truck bed, spoon as the excavator arm, and a load of sand or pasta moved one scoop at a time. Grown-up operates the site canteen; tea breaks are mandatory.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the excavator does with its arm. A dig, a scoop or a dump — any verb passes; all three is a full shift. Then listen for excavator arriving in pieces over the week.

    Parent tips

    Say both names often and let your toddler pick a favourite — the chewiness of a long word is a pleasure some toddlers refuse to give up. Freeze the digging bowl when it needs a break, not the game.

    Staying safe

    Real diggers work behind fences and hoardings for good reason — watch from outside the barrier, and keep the spoon-digger out of the dog’s bowl and the plug socket alike.

    This lesson pairs with the Excavator flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Dump Truck — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson is a transport cycle in miniature: load the box, push the load, tip it out — dump! — with the action words narrated until they belong to your toddler.

    What is this?

    A dump truck is a strong truck with a tipping back that carries loads and dumps them — the machine version of what toddlers do to every basket they meet.

    What does it mean?

    Tip and dump are action words a toddler can perform while saying them. Verb-plus-action pairs are the fastest vocabulary there is at two.

    What does the child need to know?

    The joy is the tipping moment: the pause at the top, the crash at the bottom. Narrate the cycle — it tips, it dumps, it goes again — and the words ride along.

    Why this matters

    The dump truck takes the tidying-up instinct and reverses it into a game, which makes it the rare card that requires no clean-up argument afterwards.

    What it teaches

    Action-word vocabulary (load, push, tip, dump), cause and effect in a visible loop, and the first pretend-work pride — a machine with a job.

    Words to learn

    dump truckloadtipdumpheavyagain

    Say this to your child

    “"Dump truck! It carries a big load. Fill it up… push, push… and tip it up — DUMP! Everything falls out! What shall we load next? Again, again!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say dump truck, then tip it with your hand — up, up, and DUMP, with the sound effect doing the falling.
    2. Fill a small box with soft toys, push it across the room together, then tip it: dump! Reload on request, because the reload is the game.
    3. Hunt dump trucks in books and toy boxes; every one gets a pretend load and a tip.
    4. When dump! arrives before any other word of the day, write it down mentally as a milestone — first verbs deserve the celebration.
    5. Run the load-and-dump circuit daily this week, moving the dump target to a new room each time for novelty.

    Look closer at the picture

    This card reads Dump Truck with Rumble underneath. Ask which part tips up at the back, then find the rumble word and make the noise once.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the dump truck?" "What does the back of the truck do?" "Can you say dump?" "Is the load heavy or light?"

    What your child can say or do

    "DUMP!" at the exact moment of the tip, or a full cycle performed solo with the laundry basket. The word dump entering daily speech ahead of schedule is this card’s signature.

    Out in the real world

    Real dump trucks work at roadworks and building sites, tipping gravel in slow, enormous loads. From the window or the fence, watch one tip together and narrate the whole cycle.

    Try it together

    Delivery route: load the basket at the toy corner, drive it to the sofa-depot, dump it, beep, and return empty. Four rooms, one circuit, endless freight — and the tidying is one trip backwards.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the dump truck does. A tip, a dump or a load — any action word passes. Then watch the next basket approach: if dump! is announced mid-tip, the verb is theirs now.

    Parent tips

    Narrate the cycle in the same short words every round — it loads, it tips, it dumps — because repetition with rhythm is how verbs stick. Reverse it into tidying when the day needs it; the truck will not mind.

    Staying safe

    Keep the loads soft — blocks and bricks fly at dump time. Real dump trucks stay behind site fences, and their reversing beep means stand back, a rule worth pointing out at every sighting.

    This lesson pairs with the Dump Truck flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Airplane — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson puts wings on your toddler: arms out, whoosh, a slow circuit of the room — with sky-spotting as the version of the game that works anywhere, any weather.

    What is this?

    An airplane is a machine with wide wings that flies high and goes whoosh — seen mostly as a tiny dot crossing the sky, which is exactly why the close-up card is exciting.

    What does it mean?

    The whoosh is a long, airy sound with no hard edges — sustained breath again, this time stretched across a whole room flight.

    What does the child need to know?

    Real planes are dots until suddenly they are loud. If a low flyover startles your toddler, name it calmly — that was just the airplane — and the next one is a game instead of a fright.

    Why this matters

    Arms-out flying is the biggest gesture in the set, and sky-spotting is the only vehicle hunt that needs nothing but weather and a neck crane.

    What it teaches

    Sustained breath with a long sound, big-body imitation, and sky-tracking — following a moving dot with the eyes, a genuine attention workout.

    Words to learn

    airplanewhooshflywingshighsky

    Say this to your child

    “"Airplane! Whoosh! Can you fly? Arms out wide — whoooosh, round the corner. Look up! Can you see the airplane, high in the sky? A little dot going somewhere far away."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say airplane, then whoosh — one long breath, arms spreading wide as the sound goes.
    2. Fly the room: arms as wings, leaning into gentle turns, whooshing past each other in opposite directions.
    3. Hunt airplanes in books and toys, then take the game outside or to the window and wait for the real dot to cross.
    4. When the whoosh arrives as a whistle or a hiss, take it — the long breath is the skill, and any long sound is practice.
    5. Fly once a day this week and sky-check at every outdoor pause; the dot-spotting habit outlasts the card.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card is labelled Airplane with Whoosh beneath. Find the wings stretched wide on the picture, then find the sound word and let it fly.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the airplane?" "What does the airplane say?" "Can you fly around the rug?" "Can you spot the airplane in the sky?"

    What your child can say or do

    A running "whooooosh!" with arms out, or a silent pointing finger at the ceiling. Some toddlers will land on you at the end of every flight — landings are the fun part.

    Out in the real world

    Parks, gardens and car journeys all pass under flight paths. The dot is the daily quarry; the loud low flyover is the bonus round, best met from the safety of your lap.

    Try it together

    Airport at home: a rug runway, a takeoff waddle, a whoosh lap of the room, and a landing on the cushion. Control tower duties rotate; delays are announced dramatically.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the airplane says and where it flies. A whoosh plus high or sky passes. Then watch the next outdoor pause — an upward-pointing finger before you ask is the pass with honours.

    Parent tips

    Fly slowly; fast whooshes end in collisions. When real planes startle, name then normalise in one sentence each — information first, cuddle second, and the sky stays friendly.

    Staying safe

    No real-plane notes needed — but the arms-out flying does need a clear runway, so move the coffee table and the rug-rails before takeoff.

    This lesson pairs with the Airplane flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Helicopter — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson adds a new verb to the vehicle set: hover. Spin, hover, freeze, land — the helicopter is the freeze-game champion, and stopping on cue is the hidden skill.

    What is this?

    A helicopter is a flying machine with spinning blades on top that goes whirr — and unlike every other vehicle, it can stop and hang in the air.

    What does it mean?

    Hover-and-freeze is impulse control wearing a rotor blade: the game is precisely about stopping when told, which toddlers practise harder when the stopping is funny.

    What does the child need to know?

    The blades go round and round — spin words come free with this card. Freeze mid-air like a real helicopter, then land gently; the landing is the punchline.

    Why this matters

    Freeze games are gold at two: they burn energy, teach stopping and always end in laughter. The helicopter hands you the frame; your toddler supplies the drama.

    What it teaches

    Start-and-stop body control, spinning-hand fine motor work, and sound imitation with a wobble in it — whirr is a vibrating noise worth mastering.

    Words to learn

    helicopterwhirrspinhoverfreezeland

    Say this to your child

    “"Helicopter! Whirr, whirr — round go the blades. Can you hover? Up, up… and FREEZE! Hold it… hold it… and down we come, soft landing. Whirr again!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say helicopter, then whirr — a wobbly, vibrating sound while your hands spin above your head like blades.
    2. Fly together: whirr around the room, then call freeze! and hang there mid-hover, then land softly on a cushion.
    3. Hunt helicopters in books and toys; find the spinning blades on each one and give them a twirl with your finger.
    4. When the whirr comes out as a motor hum or a raspberry, accept it and keep your hands spinning — the wobble is the character of the sound.
    5. Play one freeze round a day this week, and let your toddler call the freeze for you at least once.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look for the label Helicopter and the word Whirr below. The spinning blades sit on top — ask where they are and give them a pretend twirl.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the helicopter?" "What does the helicopter say?" "Can you freeze in the air?" "Where do the blades spin?"

    What your child can say or do

    A hovering "whirrrr" with spinning hands, or a full-body wobble freeze held for two heroic seconds. When your toddler calls freeze! and watches you obey, the game has fully hatched.

    Out in the real world

    Helicopters thrum overhead on clear days — the sound arrives first, always. Rush to the window together, whirr along with the real blades, and watch it tip away sideways.

    Try it together

    Rescue hover: a teddy is stranded on the stairs, the helicopter flies over, hovers, lowers the invisible winch (your arm), lifts the teddy and lands it safely. Freeze at the top, every time.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the helicopter says and what it can do that planes cannot. A whirr plus hover or freeze passes. The next pause-and-freeze on your word, mid-living-room, is the diploma.

    Parent tips

    Swap the caller role early — being the one who commands freeze is where the listening really happens. Keep landings soft by declaring cushions the only legal helipads.

    Staying safe

    Spinning arms in a small room meet lampshades eventually — clear the flight zone first. Real helicopters keep their distance; if one lands nearby at an event, watch from behind the barrier with everyone else.

    This lesson pairs with the Helicopter flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Boat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson sails the deck’s wettest vehicle through bath time: float, push, splash — with the boats-on-water, cars-on-roads sorting fact delivered where it sticks.

    What is this?

    A boat is a vessel that floats on water and goes splash — propelled by sails, oars or engines, and demonstrated nightly in your own bathtub.

    What does it mean?

    Boats go on water, cars go on roads: two cards, two sentences, one tidy sorting fact. Habitat talk starts with the easiest pair there is.

    What does the child need to know?

    Bath time is the daily laboratory: any plastic tub or lid becomes a boat, and one puff of breath is the wind. Splash is the sound that needs no teaching.

    Why this matters

    The boat card converts a routine into a lesson without adding a minute: the bath was happening anyway, and now it has a freight schedule.

    What it teaches

    Floating-and-sinking early science, habitat sorting (water versus road), and breath control with the sail-blowing puff.

    Words to learn

    boatsplashfloatwatersailbath

    Say this to your child

    “"A boat! It floats on the water. Can you push it? Puff, puff — here comes the wind. Splish, splash! Boats go on water. And where do cars go? On the road — not in the bath!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say boat, then splash — with both hands doing the wave.
    2. Float a plastic tub in the bath and push it across the water together; add a puff of breath on the sail if one is stuck on.
    3. Hunt boats in books and toys, then sort at the bath edge: which vehicles go on water, and which stay on the road?
    4. When splash arrives as a word, a clap or an actual wave of bathwater, take all three — the sound lives in the action.
    5. Make one bath a boat night this week and let the card watch from the towel rail; water play keeps the lesson afloat on its own.

    Look closer at the picture

    The label says Boat with the word Splash underneath. Ask what the boat is floating on, then find the splash word and wave both hands.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the boat?" "What does the boat say?" "Can you blow the sail?" "Where do boats go — the road or the water?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Splash!" with a two-hand wave, or a puff aimed at a floating lid. Expect boats in every bath for a season, with increasingly ambitious cargo.

    Out in the real world

    Ponds, rivers, harbours and rain puddles all host boats. The puddle version is the fastest: a leaf or a stick becomes a boat, and the splash is free.

    Try it together

    Cargo run: load the tub-boat with two small waterproof toys, sail it across the bath, unload at the far edge, and sail back empty. Wind provided by lungs, waves provided by elbows.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the boat says and where boats go. A splash plus water passes. Then listen at the next bath — if the sorting fact appears unprompted, the boat has delivered its cargo.

    Parent tips

    Keep one designated bath-boat permanently; ownership beats novelty. The water-versus-road sort is worth repeating with two cards each session — sorting by habitat is a big idea arriving early.

    Staying safe

    Bath supervision is eyes-on and arm’s-reach, always — splash games or not. At real ponds and harbours, hands are held and watching happens from your lap, never from the edge alone.

    This lesson pairs with the Boat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Ship — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson scales up from the boat: containers stacked high, a toot toot horn, and the big-little contrast that makes ship and boat teach each other.

    What is this?

    A ship is a huge boat that crosses the sea, stacked with containers, and it goes toot toot — the deck’s biggest water vehicle.

    What does it mean?

    Boat and ship blur at two, and that is fine: the size word does the sorting — little boat, BIG ship. Contrast vocabulary is the real lesson under the labels.

    What does the child need to know?

    Ships carry containers — stacks of boxes riding on the deck. Stacking blocks on a toy boat rebuilds the picture in three dimensions at bath time.

    Why this matters

    The ship gives the water world its giant, the same way the elephant did for animals. Sets feel complete once their biggest member has a name.

    What it teaches

    Size contrast in pairs, stacking and balance play, and the horn sound with a long tooting breath — plus first harbour-and-cargo vocabulary.

    Words to learn

    shiptootbigcontainersseaharbour

    Say this to your child

    “"A ship! Toot, toot! So big, and stacked with boxes. Next to the little boat — look! Big ship, little boat. Can you toot the horn? Nice and long: tooooooot!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say ship, then toot toot — long, low and important, with your fist on an imaginary horn cord.
    2. Put the boat card beside it and sort by size out loud: little boat, big ship. Let your toddler point to the big one.
    3. Stack a container load: blocks on a toy boat, sailed across the bath or the rug with one toot at departure.
    4. When ship comes out as bop or a toot with no word, take the toot and model ship once — the size contrast matters more than the label.
    5. Watch for real ships in books, on harbours and in the news this week, always with the size line attached.

    Look closer at the picture

    On this card the label is Ship with Toot toot beneath it. Ask what is stacked on the deck — containers are the detail the card is built on.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the ship?" "What does the ship say?" "Which is bigger, the ship or the boat?" "What is riding on the deck?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Toot toot!" with a fist-pull, or ship! reserved exclusively for the bathtub’s largest vessel. Expect every tall stack of blocks to be declared a ship — stacking is contagious.

    Out in the real world

    Harbours, ferries and canal boats bring ships close; picture books bring the container stacks. The ferry crossing or the port walk is the field trip this card hints at.

    Try it together

    Container loading: how many blocks can the toy ship carry before it tips? Load, sail, count, tip. The tipping is science, the reloading is perseverance, and the toot never gets old.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the ship says and which is bigger — ship or boat. A toot plus big passes. Then watch the block play: a tooted departure means the ship has taken the helm.

    Parent tips

    Let the size word do the heavy lifting instead of forcing the vocabulary distinction — big versus little is the age-appropriate win. Keep the block stacks low; a capsized cargo is funny once.

    Staying safe

    Real ships and ferries mean real water rules: hands held on any quay, lifejackets on boats that move, and never turned away from the water for a second at the harbour edge.

    This lesson pairs with the Ship flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Rocket — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson ends the vehicle set with a launch: the countdown, the crouch, the leap — nobody mentions that counting backwards is a real cognitive stretch; nobody has to.

    What is this?

    A rocket is a machine that blasts into the sky with a fire-roar and a whoosh — preceded by the loudest countdown in any language.

    What does it mean?

    Counting down is harder than counting up, and two-year-olds can own the last three numbers: three, two, one. It is sequencing in reverse, hidden inside a jump.

    What does the child need to know?

    The rocket pairs with the airplane for a fast-versus-far-away conversation, but honestly the countdown carries the card alone. Blast off is its own reward.

    Why this matters

    The rocket game ends in a jump, which makes it the day’s best energy valve. And the whole family shouting the countdown together is the good kind of chaos.

    What it teaches

    Backwards counting and sequencing, anticipation and waiting (the hard part before the jump), and a big whole-body launch that empties the wiggles.

    Words to learn

    rocketblast offcountdownthreetwoone

    Say this to your child

    “"Rocket! Get ready to launch. Three… two… one… BLAST OFF! Whoosh, up into the sky! Can you crouch low like a rocket on the pad? Here comes the countdown… three, two, one!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say rocket, then run the countdown — three, two, one — and blast off with a whoosh and a jump.
    2. Crouch for the countdown together, holding the crouch through three… two… one… then launch. The waiting is the workout.
    3. Hunt rockets in books and toys; every launch pad gets its countdown before the toy leaves the floor.
    4. When your toddler supplies just one! or a shriek at the jump, take it and keep counting yourself — the numbers arrive by osmosis.
    5. Run one launch a day this week, lengthening the countdown by one number only when the crouch holds steady.

    Look closer at the picture

    Find the label Rocket and the word Whoosh under it. Ask which way the rocket points — straight up is the answer the picture gives.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the rocket?" "What does the rocket say?" "Can you crouch like a rocket waiting?" "Can you count with me — three, two, one?"

    What your child can say or do

    A vibrating crouch, a shouted one!, and a vertical launch that lands hard on the cushions. Some toddlers will demand countdowns at every stairway and sofa for a fortnight.

    Out in the real world

    Rockets live in books and launches on screens — but the countdown itself is everywhere: lifts, kettles, traffic lights. Narrate the real ones; the game follows you around town.

    Try it together

    Launch pad: cushion cluster as the pad, crouch, countdown, jump to the rug-landing-zone, repeat. Rotate the count-down caller and the jump takes care of nap time by itself.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the rocket does before it flies. A countdown, a crouch or a one! all pass. Then listen for an unprompted two… one! before a jump — the sequencing has gone independent.

    Parent tips

    Keep the countdown short and sacred — three numbers is plenty, and the pause before blast off is where the learning hides. Never skip straight to the jump; the waiting IS the lesson.

    Staying safe

    Launch zones need soft landings and headroom — cushions out, ceiling fans and lampshades cleared. indoor countdowns only; the garden version waits for a clear, flat, barefoot-safe patch.

    This lesson pairs with the Rocket flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Taxi — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson hires out the yellow car: beep beep, where to, governor? — jobs-and-places pretend play with the bounciest word in the deck as the fare.

    What is this?

    A taxi is a yellow car with a sign on top that carries people where they ask to go, and it goes beep beep — the car with a job.

    What does it mean?

    Taxi is a friendly word to say — easy consonants, a bouncy rhythm. Say it slowly once: tax-eee. Words with a bounce get repeated, and repeated words get learned.

    What does the child need to know?

    Taxis are cars with a passenger service: you call, they come, you say where. If your toddler has ridden one, this card is a memory; if not, the pretend version covers it.

    Why this matters

    The pretend play has real grammar in it — destinations, passengers, stops. Saying where to go is early storytelling with a horn on it.

    What it teaches

    Pretend role-play with jobs and places, destination words (park, home, shop), and turn-taking between driver and caller.

    Words to learn

    taxibeepyellowridedriverwhere

    Say this to your child

    “"Taxi! Beep beep! Where to, today? To the park? Hop in! The taxi is yellow with a sign on top. Tax-eee — what a fun word to say. Beep beep — here we go!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say taxi, then beep beep — and say it slowly once for the bounce: tax-eee.
    2. Play taxi: one of you drives, the other calls the destination — "to the park, please!" — and off you vroom.
    3. Hunt taxis in books and from the window; the yellow paint and the little roof sign are the spot-it details.
    4. When your toddler says tac or teee, take it warmly and keep the rides going; the full word rides along on its own schedule.
    5. Run one taxi shift a day this week — destinations rotating between the door, the bath and the book corner.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card says Taxi at the top with Beep beep written beneath. Ask what colour it is painted, then hunt for the little sign on the roof.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the taxi?" "What does the taxi say?" "Can you say tax-eee, nice and slow?" "Where should the taxi take us today?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Taxi!" with a steering-wheel turn, or a destination called from the back of an armchair. Expect to be driven to the moon at least once; the fare is negotiable.

    Out in the real world

    City streets, airport queues and story books keep taxis visible. The roof sign is the real-world find-it detail — point it out at every yellow car that passes.

    Try it together

    Taxi rank: line up dolls and teddies with somewhere to be, and your toddler drives each one in turn — "where to?" — destinations called, rides delivered, fares paid in hugs.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the taxi says and where it takes people. A beep plus somewhere passes. The deeper pass: your toddler driving you somewhere and demanding a destination — caller and caller roles both working.

    Parent tips

    Rotate driver and passenger every two rounds — being asked where to go is the language-rich seat. Keep destinations real and nearby at first; the moon can wait until round five.

    Staying safe

    Real taxis need the same car-seat rules as any car — and hold hands at kerbs while hailing. Pretend taxis stop for any passenger; street taxis stop for grown-ups only.

    This lesson pairs with the Taxi flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Van — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson runs the delivery round: load the basket, beep at each door, hand over the parcel — with the van-car-truck sorting conversation kept light and honest.

    What is this?

    A van is a big boxy vehicle that carries parcels and goes beep — the machine that makes the whole street run to the window.

    What does it mean?

    Van, car, truck — three similar shapes, and toddlers enjoy the sorting once someone names the difference simply: one huge box riding on wheels.

    What does the child need to know?

    Vans bring things people ordered, which makes every delivery a small festival. If one stops at your door this week, the card has a live broadcast to watch.

    Why this matters

    The delivery game has a natural loop — load, drive, beep, hand over — that toddlers can run end to end themselves, which is rare in vehicle play.

    What it teaches

    Sorting similar vehicles, sequence play with a clear routine, and the social script of delivering — knock, hello, parcel, thank you.

    Words to learn

    vanbeepparcelboxdeliverknock

    Say this to your child

    “"A van! Beep beep — delivery! One huge box on wheels, full of parcels. Knock knock! Here is your parcel, madam. Thank you! Where next? Beep beep — off we go!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say van, then beep — one short cheerful honk, with a knock-knock on the floor for the doorstep.
    2. Load a laundry basket with parcel-soft-toys and run a delivery round: drive to a chair, knock knock, beep, hand over the parcel.
    3. Sort the fleet: van, car, truck cards in a row — which one is the big box? Keep the descriptions simple and honest.
    4. When your toddler says ban or just knocks, take it — the routine carries the word, and the word lands when it lands.
    5. Watch for the real thing: any van that stops nearby this week gets the full commentary, from beeping to parcel-handover.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look for the label Van and the word Vroom beneath. Ask what shape the van makes — one huge box riding on wheels is the honest answer to say together.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the van?" "What does the van say?" "Is the van more like a box or a ball?" "Can you knock on the door and deliver the parcel?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Beep!" with a knock-knock on the nearest table, or a parcel carried with two careful hands. Expect deliveries to every room in the house, including the loo.

    Out in the real world

    Delivery days are van days: the engine, the doors, the parcels, the beep of the locks. Watch one round from the window and narrate the whole routine as it happens.

    Try it together

    Parcel office: wrap blocks in cloths, load the van-basket, and run a full round to every family member — knock, greet, deliver, thank-you. The wrapping takes minutes and doubles the play.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the van says and what it carries. A beep plus parcels passes. Then watch the next real delivery — a knock-knock mime at the window means the routine is installed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the van-car-truck sort to one honest sentence per vehicle; precision is a grown-up hobby. The doorstep script — knock, hello, here you go — is social language hiding in a game.

    Staying safe

    Real vans reverse with blind spots and beeping warnings — hold hands in any street where one is working. At home, the parcels are soft and the knocking is on surfaces that cannot break.

    This lesson pairs with the Van flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · VEHICLES & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Scooter — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson matches the card to the machine in the shed: zoom, push, stop — the scooter is the vehicle toddlers can operate themselves, so the safety rules arrive with it.

    What is this?

    A scooter is a small ride with a handlebar and two wheels that goes zoom — pushed by one foot while the other stands and steers.

    What does it mean?

    Zoom is the sound of your own power: the scooter is the first vehicle many toddlers actually drive, and self-powered speed teaches cause and effect at knee height.

    What does the child need to know?

    Scooters and helmets go in the same sentence from the very first ride — the rule lands best arriving with the fun, not after the first tumble. One foot on, one foot push.

    Why this matters

    Owning a vehicle changes the game: this card is not about watching wheels go round, it is about being the engine, the driver and the brakes.

    What it teaches

    Balance and one-foot coordination, stop-and-go control, and rule ownership — the helmet sentence learned as part of the fun, not a tax on it.

    Words to learn

    scooterzoompushhandlebarstophelmet

    Say this to your child

    “"Scooter! Zoom! Can you push? One foot here, one foot go — zooooom! And stop! Hands on the handlebars. What do we wear on our head? Helmet first, zoom second."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say scooter, then zoom — with a forward lean and a push of one invisible foot.
    2. Practise the stance standing still: one foot here, one foot pushes, hands on the handlebar. Then zoom one rug-length with a push-along.
    3. Match card to machine: bring the card to the real scooter in the shed and find the handlebar, the wheels, the standing spot.
    4. When zoom arrives as a wheee or a shout, take it — the speed joy is the sound; the word will catch the feeling soon.
    5. Attach the rules to every ride this week: helmet on, zoom, stop at the kerb — the card rides in the basket as the checklist.

    Look closer at the picture

    The label reads Scooter with the word Zoom below it. Find the handlebar with one finger, then count how many wheels roll underneath.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the scooter?" "What does the scooter say?" "Which foot pushes?" "What do we put on before we zoom?"

    What your child can say or do

    "Zoom!" at takeoff, wheee at the corners, and stop! rehearsed at every doorway. Expect the helmet sentence repeated back to you verbatim by the end of the week — rules copy well when they ride on fun.

    Out in the real world

    Parks, pavements and the school run are scooter territory. Real riders zip past wearing real helmets — every one is a billboard for the rule.

    Try it together

    Stop-and-zoom street: cushions mark the kerbs, and the scooter rider must stop completely at each one before zooming on. The stopping is harder than the zooming, which is exactly the point.

    Understanding check

    Ask what the scooter says and what comes first, helmet or zoom. A zoom plus helmet passes fully. The live test is the next real ride: a standing wait at the cushion-kerb without being told.

    Parent tips

    Let the helmet be the ignition key — no helmet, no zoom, said cheerfully a hundred times. Practise the stance off the scooter first; balance arrives faster barefoot on the rug.

    Staying safe

    Helmet on before wheels move, closed shoes, and flat ground only at two — slopes come later. Scooters stay off roads and driveways entirely; pavements and parks are the whole map for now.

    This lesson pairs with the Scooter flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Vehicles & Sounds (Toddler 6).
